note.note:
History:
- Chief complaint: Painful, stinging/burning urination for a few days with lower abdominal (suprapubic) crampy pain.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began a few days ago and have been ongoing; described as bothersome but not unbearable.
- Associated findings: Small amount of visible blood in urine earlier today; urine has an unusual/“weird” smell. No increased urinary frequency or urgency reported. No vaginal discharge noticed. No fevers, no flank/back pain, no nausea or vomiting.
- Context/sex history: 19-year-old sexually active female with a single boyfriend for a couple of months; uses condoms; reports never having had an STI screen.
- Self-treatment: Tried over-the-counter bicarbonate a few days ago without benefit.

Past Medical History:
- IBS (irritable bowel syndrome).
- Allergies: Clindamycin — causes swelling.
- Medications: No regular medications. Recently tried OTC bicarbonate (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Physical Examination:
- Formal vital signs and physical exam: Not recorded.
- Relevant history-based findings and negatives:
  - No fever reported.
  - No flank or back pain.
  - No vaginal discharge.
  - Bowels reported as working normally.
- Note: Clinician stated plan to examine but no recorded exam findings.

Impression:
- Primary impression: Probable acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection) — clinical presentation (dysuria, suprapubic cramp, malodorous urine, brief visible hematuria) consistent with clinician’s assessment.
- Other plausible diagnoses consistent with transcript:
  - Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — sexually active, never screened; can present with dysuria and minimal discharge (medium likelihood).
  - Urolithiasis (lower urinary tract stone) — hematuria and dysuria can arise from a stone (low–medium likelihood).

Management Plan:
- Immediate/acute treatment advised by clinician:
  - Empiric oral antibiotic therapy planned: Either nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim; regimen discussed as "one tablet twice daily for 3 days." (Exact antibiotic choice and tablet strength not documented.)
  - Advise increased oral fluids to help flush the urinary tract.
  - Cranberry juice suggested as possibly helpful for symptoms.
  - Recommend avoiding sexual intercourse while symptomatic; continue barrier contraception if used.
- Safety net / return precautions:
  - Return or contact clinician if not improved by the end of the week.
  - Seek prompt care if fever, flank/back pain, or worsening systemic illness develop (concern for ascending infection/pyelonephritis).
- Additional recommendations (supported by transcript context and DDx):
  - Consider pregnancy test if there is any concern about pregnancy (clinician advised this as appropriate in young females).
  - Consider STI testing (urine NAAT for chlamydia/gonorrhea) given sexual activity and no prior screening — clinician elicited sexual history and screening status; testing not documented as ordered.
  - If symptoms persist or recur, obtain urine dipstick/urinalysis and urine culture; consider further evaluation (including imaging) if stone suspected or if symptoms worsen.

Patient Summary:
- 19-year-old sexually active female with several days of dysuria, suprapubic crampy pain, malodorous urine, and a small episode of visible hematuria. Clinician assessed this as most consistent with an acute uncomplicated urinary tract infection and planned empiric oral antibiotics plus supportive measures, with instructions to re-contact if symptoms worsen or fail to improve.

Key Takeaways (patient instructions):
- Start the prescribed antibiotic course (nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim as discussed), one tablet twice daily for 3 days (med choice/strength not documented).
- Drink plenty of fluids and avoid sex until symptoms resolve; continue using barrier contraception if in use.
- Return or call if you develop fever, flank pain, feel more unwell, or if symptoms have not improved by the end of the week.

Next Steps:
- Confirm which antibiotic will be dispensed (nitrofurantoin vs trimethoprim) and verify tablet strength/complete dosing instructions at pharmacy.
- Consider point-of-care urine dipstick/urinalysis and urine culture if symptoms persist or recur.
- Consider urine NAAT testing for chlamydia/gonorrhea given sexual history (patient reports never screened).
- Pregnancy test if there is any concern for pregnancy.
- Re-evaluation if fever, flank pain, or worsening symptoms (possible upper tract involvement).

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: documented vital signs; formal physical examination findings; urine dipstick/urinalysis results; urine culture results; pregnancy test result; explicit prescription details (selected antibiotic name, tablet strength, route/confirmation of dispense); documentation of STI testing ordered or performed.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted — DDx ranking (acute cystitis highest) aligns with clinician assessment in transcript.
- Transcript quality: Audio/dialogue mostly clear; some overlapping speech and brief inaudible portions but clinical data extraction feasible.
